spoken_claim: Apollo astronauts left special reflectors on the lunar surface
value_and_source: Apollo 11 and 14: 100 fused-silica corner cubes, 3.8 cm each, 46 cm aluminium panel; Apollo 15: 300 cubes (hexagonal/honeycomb pattern). Sites: Sea of Tranquility, Fra Mauro, Hadley Rille. ILRS Apollo and Luna Reflectors page https://ilrs.gsfc.nasa.gov/missions/satellite_missions/current_missions/ap11_reflector.html (read in browser); UCSD Lunar Retroreflectors page https://tmurphy.physics.ucsd.edu/apollo/lrrr.html (read by a subagent). Also French-built 14-cube arrays on Luna 17 and 21
assumptions_and_gaps: Apollo 11 deployed by Buzz Aldrin on 1969-07-21 (JPL caption and Wikipedia via search results; not yet read on the primary page)
rule_for_picture: Show three Apollo arrays in the manifest; the film needs one (Apollo 11, Sea of Tranquility, matches the B05 ring); do not name astronauts on screen until the primary page is read

spoken_claim: They redirect a tiny fraction of incoming light back toward where it came from
status: AMBIGUOUS, defensible with the right picture (softened from the first draft)
value_and_source: Corner cubes "return any incident light back in exactly the direction from which it came" (UCSD Lunar Retroreflectors page https://tmurphy.physics.ucsd.edu/apollo/lrrr.html (read by a subagent)). The array intercepts only a tiny part of the beam: "a one-in-25-million chance of a photon launched from Earth finding the Apollo 11 reflector"; a 1 arcsec beam spreads to 1.9 km at the Moon (Murphy 2013 Rep. Prog. Phys. 76, 076901, arXiv:1309.6294 (text read by a subagent via ar5iv; sections cited) Secs 1.2-1.3)
assumptions_and_gaps: Spoken as "redirect a tiny fraction of incoming light" it can be heard as "the reflector sends back only a little of what it receives", which is wrong. It is right if "incoming light" means the whole beam
rule_for_picture: Owner decision 2026-11-26: keep the recorded line. spoken_claim: Almost none of the light makes it back to the detector
value_and_source: Up-leg about 4e-8 onto Apollo 11/14 arrays; down-leg: a 1 m aperture receives about 5e-9 of the flux at the reflector; net about 2e-16 for 1 m, total throughput near 1e-18 after atmosphere, optics and detection (Murphy 2013 Rep. Prog. Phys. 76, 076901, arXiv:1309.6294 (text read by a subagent via ar5iv; sections cited) Sec 1.3). The down-leg spread is set by diffraction from the corner cubes
assumptions_and_gaps: figures are for specific apertures and conditions
rule_for_picture: On screen: two widening cones and tiny discs, no numbers (ratios are too small to draw to scale). If one number is wanted: "one in 25 million photons even finds the reflector"

spoken_claim: Scientists collect just a few returning photons from many laser pulses
value_and_source: APOLLO 3.5 m, 5000-shot runs: Apollo 15 3.15 photons/shot, Apollo 14 1.52, Apollo 11 0.96 (Murphy 2013 Rep. Prog. Phys. 76, 076901, arXiv:1309.6294 (text read by a subagent via ar5iv; sections cited) Table 2). Smaller telescopes: 0.002 to 0.2 photons per pulse (Sec 3.1). Laser: 532 nm, about 90 ps pulses, 115 mJ, 20 Hz (Murphy et al. 2008 PASP, APOLLO instrument paper, arXiv:0710.0890 (read by a subagent via ar5iv, sections 1-3.3 verbatim) Sec 3.1). Photon-regime statement: LLR "invariably operates in the single-photon detection regime" (Sec 1.3)
assumptions_and_gaps: "few per pulse" is right for the best station and best target; most stations see far fewer per pulse
rule_for_picture: Histogram counts labelled illustrative; three dots for "A few photons" is fine

spoken_claim: They even account for the effects of Earth's atmosphere
value_and_source: About 1.5 m of zenith delay at high-altitude sites; pressure measured to 0.1 mbar is enough to model it to about 1 mm (Murphy et al. 2008 PASP, APOLLO instrument paper, arXiv:0710.0890 (read by a subagent via ar5iv, sections 1-3.3 verbatim) Sec 1.3); Murphy 2013 Sec 5.1: roughly 2 m path delay that must be determined and removed
assumptions_and_gaps: the correction method in Murphy Sec 5.3-5.4 was NOT read verbatim
rule_for_picture: Show a delay and a correction tick, not a number, unless 1.5 m is wanted and attributed

spoken_claim: Let them measure the distance with remarkable precision
value_and_source: 1 mm of one-way range = 6.7 ps of round-trip time (Murphy et al. 2008 PASP, APOLLO instrument paper, arXiv:0710.0890 (read by a subagent via ar5iv, sections 1-3.3 verbatim) Sec 2.1; our derivation 6.671 ps). APOLLO claims "one-millimeter range precision" (abstract, 2008); Murphy 2013 reports a median statistical uncertainty per normal point under 3 mm and range precision "a few millimeters recently"; a 200 ps single-photon spread needs about 900 photons for 1 mm (Sec 1.3)
rule_for_picture: One on-screen figure allowed: "about 1 millimetre = 7 trillionths of a second" (6.7 ps)
